PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Liu et al Original Paper Reliability of Large Language Model Generated Clinical Reasoning in Assisted Reproductive Technology: Blinded Comparative Evaluation Study Dou Liu1,2,3*, BSc; Ying Long1,3,4*, MD; Sophia Zuoqiu5, PhD; Di Liu5,6,7, PhD; Kang Li6,7, PhD; Yiting Lin8, MBBS; Hanyi Liu8, MBBS; Rong Yin5,6,7*, PhD; Tian Tang1,3,4*, MD 1Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, West China Second University Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 2Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States 3Key Laboratory of Birth Defects and Related Diseases of Women and Children, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 4Reproductive Medical Center, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, West China Second University Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 5Department of Industrial Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 6West China Biomedical Big Data Center, West China Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 7Med-X Center for Informatics, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China 8West China School of Medicine, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China *these authors contributed equally Corresponding Author: Tian Tang, MD Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology West China Second University Hospital of Sichuan University Chengdu China Phone: 1 18081110066 Email: tiantang2016@scu.edu.cn Abstract Background: High-quality clinical chains-of-thought (CoTs) are essential for explainable medical artificial intelligence (AI); yet, their development is limited by data scarcity. Large language models can generate medical CoTs, but their clinical reliability is unclear. Objective: We evaluated the clinical reliability of large language model–generated CoTs in reproductive medicine and examined prompting strategies to improve their quality. Methods: In a blinded comparative study at a clinical center, senior clinicians in assisted reproductive technology evaluated CoTs generated via 3 distinct strategies: zero-shot, random few-shot (using random shallow examples), and selective few-shot (using diverse, high-quality examples). Expert ratings were then compared with evaluations from a state-of-the-art AI model (GPT-4o). Results: The selective few-shot strategy significantly outperformed other strategies across logical clarity, use of key information, and clinical accuracy (P<.001). Critically, the random few-shot strategy offered no significant improvement over the zero-shot baseline, demonstrating that low-quality examples are as ineffective as no examples. The success of the selective strategy is attributed to 2 preliminary frameworks: “gold-standard depth” and “representative diversity.” Notably, the AI evaluator failed to discern these critical performance differences. Thus, clinical reliability depends on strategic prompt design rather than simply adding examples. Conclusions: We propose a “dual principles” preliminary framework for generating trustworthy CoTs at scale in assisted reproductive technology. This work is a preliminary step toward addressing the data bottleneck in reproductive medicine. It also underscores the essential role of human expertise in evaluating generated clinical data. JSON: Name: selective_fewshot_art_cot Title: Selective few-shot prompting to improve reliability of large language model–generated clinical chain-of-thought in assisted reproductive technology Short Hypothesis: Providing selective few-shot exemplars that combine gold-standard depth and representative diversity in prompts causes a statistically significant increase in LLM-generated clinical chain-of-thought reliability (measured by LCC, UCKI, and PCAR) compared with zero-shot and random few-shot prompting. Related Work: Prior work has shown that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and few-shot in-context learning can improve LLM performance on multi-step reasoning tasks; specialized medical LLM fine-tuning and synthetic data generation have been proposed to address data scarcity in clinical domains. Existing approaches include zero-shot CoT prompting, random in-domain few-shot prompting, synthetic EHR/narrative generation with LLMs, and automated LLM-based graders for output quality. Limitations in current methods are: (1) few-shot benefits depend heavily on exemplar quality and selection but selection strategies are underexplored in clinical settings; (2) random or shallow exemplars can fail to improve and may degrade domain-specific reasoning; (3) automated evaluators often display ceiling effects and fail to detect clinically important errors; (4) most evaluations lack blinded, clinician-led assessment and detailed metrics that separate logical coherence, information use, and clinical plausibility; (5) generalization across ART subtypes and different LLM families remains unverified. Abstract: Problem: Generating high-quality, explainable clinical chains-of-thought (CoTs) with large language models (LLMs) is a potential solution to the data bottleneck for explainable medical AI, but the clinical reliability of synthetic CoTs and the effect of exemplar selection strategies are unclear. Proposed approach: Develop and evaluate a prompting framework that contrasts zero-shot, random few-shot, and a curated selective few-shot strategy characterized by 'gold-standard depth' and 'representative diversity' of exemplars. Main contribution: A blinded, clinician-led comparative evaluation protocol that quantifies CoT reliability across three orthogonal metrics—logical coherence and clarity (LCC), use and coverage of key information (UCKI), and plausibility and clinical accuracy of reasoning (PCAR)—and demonstrates whether selective exemplar curation materially improves clinical reasoning quality. Expected outcome: Empirical evidence on the causal effect of exemplar selection on CoT reliability in assisted reproductive technology (ART), identification of exemplar design principles for trustworthy synthetic clinical reasoning, and an evaluation of automated LLM-based graders' limitations when compared with human experts. Experiments: Datasets: Deidentified ART clinical cases (N=200) drawn from a manually curated EHR dataset with structured baseline variables and unstructured history; subgroup counts: IVF n=140, ICSI n=38, PGT n=22. Generation models: primary LLM DeepSeek-R1-671b (consistent with prior work); secondary models for generalization: GPT-4o and an open-weight Llama-family model. Prompting conditions (within-case paired design): (A) zero-shot (instruction only), (B) random few-shot (5 randomly sampled shallow exemplars per prompt, excluded evaluation cases), (C) selective few-shot (6 curated exemplars with gold-standard depth and representative diversity). Ablation studies: (1) exemplar number ablation: 3 vs 5 vs 6 exemplars; (2) exemplar depth ablation: deep (multi-step expert CoT) vs shallow (concise CoT); (3) diversity ablation: diverse (covering ART subtypes) vs homogeneous (single subtype); (4) model ablation across the three LLMs; (5) decoding temperature: 0.0, 0.2, 0.5. Generation settings: max tokens=5000, otherwise identical. Evaluation protocol: blinded, randomized case order; two independent board-certified ART clinicians rate each generated CoT on 5-point Likert scales across three metrics: LCC, UCKI, PCAR; adjacent agreement and raw disagreement recorded; automated evaluation via GPT-4o using identical rubric. Baselines: zero-shot and random few-shot. Primary endpoints: mean paired differences in LCC, UCKI, PCAR between selective few-shot and (i) zero-shot and (ii) random few-shot. Secondary endpoints: subgroup effects by ART type, interrater agreement statistics (adjacent agreement, linear weighted kappa), AI grader sensitivity (ability to detect human-identified differences). Statistical tests: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for paired comparisons; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across multiple comparisons; report Cohen's d for paired designs; target significance α=0.05 (FDR-adjusted). Power: planned to detect Cohen d=0.3 with N=200 paired samples (power ≈0.80) for primary comparisons. Reporting: per-case qualitative error taxonomy, confusion matrices for AI grader vs clinician labels, and ablation effect-size estimates. Risk Factors and Limitations: Single-center dataset and modest subgroup sizes (PGT n=22) limit external validity and statistical power for less frequent ART subtypes; use of a single primary LLM constrains generalizability across model families; exemplar selection covaries with exemplar number and depth in the selective condition, complicating causal attribution without strict ablation controls; automated AI graders may exhibit ceiling effects and fail to detect clinically meaningful reasoning errors, compromising automated QA; LLM failure modes include hallucination, omission of critical clinical facts, and inappropriate clinical recommendations; human evaluator bias and limited rater pool (two clinicians) may produce residual subjective variability; blinded evaluation may not capture downstream clinical safety outcomes; computational costs and token limits constrain exemplar quantity and prompt engineering choices; privacy and data governance constraints restrict dataset sharing and multicenter replication; results may not generalize to other medical specialties or to deployed clinical decision-support contexts.
